deliverables.content:
Objective deliverable

Launch-week social media plan — Somebody
Status: Draft for review only; not scheduled, sent, or published.

Purpose
Address the launch brief’s identified problems: weak signup conversion, unclear recognition that Somebody is for founders running very small companies, and generic “AI manager” / “automate your workflows” language. The plan uses practical, outcome-focused messaging and does not claim that Somebody replaces the founder or guarantees a business result.

Evidence basis
- Somebody is an AI manager for founders running one-person companies and lean teams. It is intended to help organise work, bring in outside help when needed, and stay with an objective until there is a usable result. [Company profile, company/profile]
- The product is for founders who personally carry several parts of the business and need important work to keep moving without adding another tool to manage. [Company profile, company/profile]
- Signup conversion is weak, visitors do not immediately recognise the target audience or the difference from other AI tools, and current broad positioning may be too generic. The company does not yet have strong evidence for the words founders themselves use. [Launch brief, launch/context]

Launch-week messaging spine
Primary audience: founders running one-person companies and lean teams.
Core message for review: “Somebody helps founders keep important work moving—organising the work, bringing in help when needed, and staying with the objective.”
Supporting angles:
1. Name the audience plainly: “Built for founders carrying several parts of the business.”
2. Show the practical outcome: “Keep an important objective moving without adding another tool to manage.”
3. Explain the distinction: focus on responsibility and follow-through, not vague automation claims.
4. Use a low-pressure call to action such as “See how it works” or “Try Somebody,” subject to confirmation of the actual destination and offer.
Avoid: “replaces the founder,” guaranteed results, unsupported productivity claims, invented customer outcomes, or unvalidated claims about what founders commonly say.

Posting priority
P1 — Clarify who Somebody is for and the problem it addresses.
P2 — Demonstrate the practical workflow or responsibility model with a concrete, reviewable example.
P3 — Invite questions and collect language/objections for later message validation.
Priority order is a planning recommendation, not a result derived from channel-performance data.

Channel plan

TikTok
- Format: short vertical video (15–45 seconds), with on-screen text and a simple founder scenario; optional product walkthrough only if approved assets and a working flow are available.
- Priority: P1 first, then P2. Open with the audience/problem rather than “AI manager.”
- Messaging: “When you are the person carrying every important part of the business, Somebody helps keep one objective moving.” Show a before/after task sequence without promising a business result.
- Sequence: audience/problem explainer; concrete responsibility/workflow example; question-led response video based only on real comments received.
- Not responsibly specified: posting times, trend/audio choices, expected reach, or performance benchmarks without channel data and a launch calendar.

Instagram
- Format: Reels for concise demonstrations; carousel for “who it is for / how it differs / what it does not promise”; Stories for questions and review prompts.
- Priority: P1 and P2, with the profile bio and link destination reviewed before approval.
- Messaging: lead with “For founders running a one-person company or lean team,” then explain that Somebody organises work, can bring in outside help when needed, and stays with the objective.
- Sequence: positioning Reel; educational carousel; Story question box asking which important objective is hardest to keep moving. Treat responses as research, not proof of a general market pattern.
- Not responsibly specified: hashtag set, optimal cadence, audience targeting, or conversion forecast without account analytics, audience research, and confirmed landing-page details.

Facebook
- Format: short native video, concise explanatory post, and discussion prompt; use link posts only after the destination and CTA are confirmed.
- Priority: P1 clarity and trust, then P3 discussion.
- Messaging: “Somebody is for founders who personally carry several parts of the business and need important work to keep moving without another tool to manage.”
- Sequence: audience/use-case post; practical example; moderated discussion prompt about keeping an important objective moving.
- Not responsibly specified: community groups, paid targeting, demographic assumptions, posting times, or engagement targets without approved audience and distribution evidence.

X
- Format: concise text posts, short thread, reply-led conversation, and approved product visual if available.
- Priority: P1 message testing and P3 listening; keep claims narrow and concrete.
- Messaging: test variants around “built for one-person companies,” “keep an objective moving,” and “practical follow-through,” without presenting any variant as validated founder language.
- Sequence: concise positioning post; short thread explaining the responsibility model; question inviting founders to describe what currently gets stuck. Record replies for qualitative review.
- Not responsibly specified: posting frequency, hashtags, influencer amplification, expected impressions, or winning copy without account history and audience evidence.

Proposed seven-day review schedule (not a publishing instruction)
Day 1: approve audience definition, core message, landing-page destination, and CTA.
Day 2: review a TikTok/Reel-style audience/problem concept.
Day 3: review an Instagram/Facebook explanatory carousel or post.
Day 4: review the X positioning post and thread.
Day 5: review a concrete workflow example across selected channels.
Day 6: review questions/objections gathered from approved conversations.
Day 7: compare approved qualitative feedback and decide which messages merit further testing.
Weekday/date, times, volume, assets, and publication approvals are intentionally unspecified.

Assumptions requiring review
- The launch week has seven working days available for preparation or publication.
- Suitable product screenshots, demonstrations, brand assets, links, and a confirmed CTA may be supplied before approval.
- The team can review responses without treating a small social sample as representative research.
These are planning assumptions, not company-record facts.

Evidence gaps and decisions needed
No channel analytics, audience demographics, prior post performance, platform account status, launch date, posting windows, creative inventory, confirmed offer, or landing-page URL were supplied. No validated founder interviews, social listening, or approved customer proof were supplied; the company explicitly says it lacks strong evidence for founders’ own wording. Therefore this document cannot responsibly set exact dates/times, posting volume, hashtags, paid distribution, forecasted results, testimonials, or final copy claims.

Approval checklist
Confirm launch dates and channel ownership; provide approved creative assets and destination URL; confirm CTA and offer; validate product/demo details; set a measurement plan; and approve final copy before anything is scheduled or published.

Source references
- Company profile — company/profile
- Launch brief — launch/context

Version 3 review note
Revalidated the plan against the observed company profile and launch brief. No channel-specific recommendations were expanded beyond supplied evidence; unsupported dates, cadence, performance claims, audience assumptions, and final publication details remain explicitly unspecified.
